claims.text: High-temperature mechanical and thermoelastic behavior in refractory HEAs is governed by the interaction of lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion.
Lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion enhance creep resistance in refractory HEAs relative to conventional alloys.
Lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion reduce thermal expansion in refractory HEAs relative to conventional alloys.
The proposed initial material is an equiatomic refractory HEA with a homogeneous microstructure.
Atomic-radius mismatch can be varied through compositional changes while retaining equiatomic compositions.
Changing atomic-radius mismatch produces controlled variation in lattice distortion.
The proposed behavior applies under constant stress and thermal cycling at temperatures above 1000 degrees Celsius.
Lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
Lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
Higher barriers to dislocation motion and atomic diffusion reduce elevated-temperature creep rates.
Higher barriers associated with lattice distortion reduce thermal expansion coefficients at elevated temperatures.
Refractory HEAs with greater atomic-radius mismatch will have lower creep rates than lower-mismatch alloys under identical high-temperature conditions.
Refractory HEAs with greater atomic-radius mismatch will have lower thermal expansion coefficients than lower-mismatch alloys under identical high-temperature conditions.
Conventional single-phase refractory alloys containing similarly sized atoms provide a minimal-lattice-distortion baseline.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to equiatomic or near-equiatomic refractory HEAs above 1000 degrees Celsius.
A systematic series of higher- and lower-mismatch refractory HEAs can be compared using identical creep and thermal-expansion tests.
Failure of higher-mismatch alloys to show both lower creep rates and lower thermal expansion coefficients would falsify the hypothesis.
